content:
The Mathlib Initiative launched in September 2025, a bit more than a year ago. We started with a small team of 5 employees, that has since grown significantly. Our plans for year 1 were laid out in our roadmap. As we are starting the final quarter of 2026, it is a good moment to reflect on the first year of the MI, what has been accomplished, and where we've needed to adjust our plans.

Initially, we worked on four thematic areas:

  1. Review of Mathlib PRs
  2. Ecosystem infrastructure
  3. Documentation
  4. AI integration

D1. Review

Review of community contributions is a crucial ingredient for Mathlib's growth. I want to give a huge shout out to the review team at the Mathlib Initiative, who provide essential review capacity next to the community team of volunteer reviewers.

One of the main goals of the Mathlib Initiative is to streamline this review process. Since Mathlib has thousands of open pull requests in various states of completion, the reviewers look at a subset of pull requests that satisfy several criteria such as passing continuous integration testing. This subset is known as "the queue" and pull requests can go through several iterations of review, being on the queue while waiting for review, and off the queue when waiting for the author to process reviewer feedback. The queue can be visualized using the Queueboard, whose backend Bryan Gin-ge Chen has completely rewritten so that it can handle large volumes of data reliably. Thomas Murrills wrote several linters that help improve code quality and thereby automate part of the review process. He also refactored #find_home to make it compatible with the new module system.

In our initial plans for the Mathlib Initiative, we set ourselves the goal to have "review response times under one week maintained consistently for 90% of review cycles". Here, a review cycle is one of the iterations that a pull request spends on the queue, as mentioned above.

This goal was too ambitious, and was not hit, as these charts show, but it was a valuable target. Throughout 2026, the duration of review cycles has been trending upwards. At the time of writing, about 75% of review cycles are completed within 30 days, and 90% within 60 days. Improving review bandwidth is a never-ending task, and we continue to work on ways to speed-up the review process. In particular, we are looking to hire expert Mathlib contributors as contractors on the Mathlib Initiative review team.

D2. Ecosystem infrastructure

Marcelo Lynch built Hopscotch and downstream-reports to provide tooling that helps with migrating Lean projects to new versions of Lean and Mathlib. He has also significantly tightened the security of our continuous integration and build servers. Bryan wrote a security policy that outlines responsible disclosure of security issues for community infrastructure. Due to the heightened interest in Lean and Mathlib over the past months, cache usage has exploded. Marcelo has migrated the cache to a new system on CloudFlare, that has free egress and is easier to scale for the future.

D3. Documentation

Anne Baanen started the documentation effort by cataloguing all the various pieces of documentation that the community had produced over the past years: https://leanprover-community.github.io/documentation.html Subsequently, Anne developed a style guide for tactic documentation, in collaboration with the Lean FRO; and then ensured that all Mathlib's tactics were documentated accordingly. Anne launched the Mathlib Phrasebook in May. It is steadily growing with contributions arriving from MI employees and the community. Anne has also invested in preparing Mathlib docstrings for migration to the Verso system developed by the Lean FRO. We expect the migration to take place in the upcoming months.

D4. AI integration

Adam Topaz wrote LeanScout to extract various datasets from Mathlib, which are available on HuggingFace. In April we also launched Formal Frontier with the goal of autoformalizing reusable libraries that close the gap between Mathlib and frontier maths research.

D5. Computational methods

Besides these four thematic areas, we also received further funding from the Alfred P. Sloan foundation in April 2026. With this funding we have started a computational methods project, with the goal of developing a suite of tactics and verified algorithms to support computations in/with Mathlib. After ramping up, Paul Cadman and Rao Xiaojia have now built several tactics for computational linear algebra and David Ledvinka has contributed a tactic for interval arithmetic.

D0. Community support

In February 2026, I attended a retreat organized by Renaissance Philanthropy. During this meeting, I realized that the Mathlib Initiative has the opportunity to do more than technical work on reviews, infrastructure, etc. We've created a new thematic area, on the topic of community support. Concretely, we've started with three things: Thomas has started the Meta Cafe: a weekly online meeting where community members learn from each other about metaprogramming. Michael Rothgang works as community coordinator, and particularly helps organize and facilitate Mathlib maintainer meetings as well as the ongoing discussion about several aspects of community governance. Rob Lewis is leading the organization of Mathlib's 10th anniversary conference, taking place in July 2027.

Renaissance Philanthropy

Finally, I want to thank Renaissance Philanthropy for their fantastic support during this first year: launching, hiring, finances, legal, fundraising, the whole business end of running a team. The framework they provide, allows the team at the Mathlib Initiative to devote their time and energy to all the technical aspects described above.

My favorite thing about this first year of the Mathlib Initiative is the ways it's helped the ecosystem at large. I think I've said so already, but just to reiterate my thanks for projects that have most directly been helpful for me:

  • @Marcelo Lynch's work is well-designed, made with community input, and saved me a lot of time and effort. Along with complementary work from @Joscha Mennicken at the FRO, I feel like this year it has become much easier for projects that want to stay on the bleeding edge of core Lean and Mathlib.
  • @Michael Rothgang's work on governance is a challenging interpersonal effort and a time investment that is not always widely visible. In my opinion they've thoughtfully navigated this in a way I am very grateful for.
  • Having @Thomas Murrills and others (@Robin Arnez, @Jovan Gerbscheid) at the Meta Cafe is hugely useful for folks like myself at the "advanced beginner" stage of metaprogramming. I think sharing this sort of knowledge that mostly lives in people's heads is a great investment in Lean's future

I think it would also be interesting to see some charts of PR statistics relating to "maintainer merge". For example, what proportion of merged PRs have gone through maintainer-merge state first, how long do they spend in that state, how big does the backlog of PRs in maintainer-merge state get?

Such statistics are definitely available, @Bryan Gin-ge Chen has done the analysis most recently. My rule of thumb is that about every third merged PR is maintainer merged at least once before that. (Most PRs only get maintainer merged once. Some PRs get merged directly (e.g., if it was easy enough, or a maintainer takes the final look before a reviewer could), but this shows this system already helping quite a lot with distributing work.

With the caveat that I haven't yet had a chance to edit out most of the AI-generated text, this interactive page has a number of diagrams and plots that depict various aspects of the "lifecycle" of a mathlib4 PR.

To answer your specific questions, for PRs opened between 2024-02-15 (roughly when maintainer-merge was introduced) and 2026-09-30:
Joseph Myers said:

For example, what proportion of merged PRs have gone through maintainer-merge state first, how long do they spend in that state, how big does the backlog of PRs in maintainer-merge state get?

Regarding the proportion, reading numbers off the Sankey chart and the in/out flow chart beneath it: there were 25710 merged PRs and (separately) 9778 PRs that were labeled maintainer-merge (MM) at some point. 99 MM PRs have been closed without merging, 96 are still open, so 9583 / 25710 or roughly 37% of merged PRs went through MM first.

Regarding the duration that PRs spend in MM, here's one of the histograms on the page showing the amount of time PRs spend in the transition from MM to ready-to-merge (note that the x-axis is logarithmic):

The median time is 0.30 days = 7.2 hours, though because of the logarithmic scale, the half of the PRs above the median spend a lot, lot more time waiting!

I haven't looked at the size of the backlog over time, but I could try to put that together if there's interest. There are a few other interactive notebooks here (same disclaimer about them being unpolished holds) and the repo which includes code for getting data from our public queueboard exports is here.

Johan Commelin said:

we set ourselves the goal to have "review response times under one week maintained consistently for 90% of review cycles"

Do we have a (probably less ambitous) goal for the next year on review cycle?
Hold your breath for a few hours, we plan to post our roadmap for the next 6 months later today.
It just went live: https://mathlib-initiative.org/roadmap/. Please discuss at #general > Discussion: Mathlib Initiative roadmap (Oct26 - Mar27)
